introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Justify the view that after 1990 the trend of events in South Africa was towards the dismantling of Apartheid.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Apartheid, the system of institutionalised racial segregation and white minority rule introduced by the National Party after 1948, had been defended through laws such as the Population Registration Act, the Group Areas Act and the Bantustan policy. By the late 1980s, the system was in crisis because of internal resistance, economic problems and international pressure. After 1990 the trend was clearly towards the dismantling of apartheid, which culminated in the democratic elections of April 1994, although the process was marked by violence and difficulties.

**1. Background: why change became possible.** Mass resistance (the 1976 Soweto uprising, the United Democratic Front, strikes and township revolts in the 1980s), the armed struggle of the ANC, international sanctions and isolation (the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986, the arms embargo, sports boycotts), economic stagnation, and the end of the Cold War (which removed the "communist threat" argument) made the system unsustainable. F. W. de Klerk, who became president in 1989, accepted that negotiation was necessary.

**2. Evidence of the dismantling of apartheid after 1990**

*a) Removal of the political barriers (1990).* On 2 February 1990, de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC, the PAC and the South African Communist Party and other organisations, promised the release of political prisoners, and the state of emergency was lifted later in 1990. Nelson Mandela was freed on 11 February 1990 after 27 years in prison. The Groote Schuur Minute (May 1990) and the Pretoria Minute (August 1990) paved the way for talks, in which the ANC suspended the armed struggle.

*b) Repeal of the apartheid laws (1990-91).* The Separate Amenities Act was repealed in 1990, and in June 1991 parliament repealed the Land Acts, the Group Areas Act and the Population Registration Act, the pillars of the system.

*c) Negotiations on a new constitution.* The Convention for a Democratic South Africa (CODESA) opened in December 1991. After deadlock and violence (the Boipatong massacre of June 1992, the Bisho shooting in September 1992), talks resumed with the Record of Understanding (September 1992) and the Multi-Party Negotiating Forum (1993). In March 1992, white voters approved the reforms in a referendum by a large majority. In 1993 an interim constitution was agreed that provided for a non-racial democracy, a Government of National Unity and a bill of rights. Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.

*d) The first multiracial elections (April 1994).* On 26-29 April 1994, all South Africans voted for the first time. The ANC won about 62 per cent of the votes, and Mandela became president on 10 May 1994, heading a Government of National Unity that included de Klerk's National Party (which left it in 1996) and the Inkatha Freedom Party. The homelands were reincorporated into South Africa.

*e) Reconciliation and the new order.* The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (set up by an Act of 1995 and chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu) investigated apartheid-era abuses; a new constitution was adopted in 1996, guaranteeing equality; South Africa rejoined the Commonwealth and the international community, sanctions were lifted and the country returned to international sport.

**3. Difficulties and limits.** Violence between the ANC and Inkatha in Natal and the Transvaal, the assassination of the ANC leader Chris Hani (April 1993), white right-wing resistance (the AWB, the Conservative Party), and the Bophuthatswana crisis (March 1994) threatened the process. Accusations of a "third force" implicated elements of the security forces. Economic inequality persisted after 1994, so the dismantling of legal apartheid did not at once end its social and economic effects. These difficulties did not reverse the trend, however.

**Conclusion.** The view is justified. After 1990, the legal and political structures of apartheid were systematically removed through the unbanning of the liberation movements, the release of Mandela, the repeal of the major apartheid laws, negotiations and the democratic elections of 1994. Despite violence and lasting inequalities, the overall trend was clearly the dismantling of apartheid.
